passage: Chandrika's last reply to Minakshi was a thumbs-up on Monday, and by Friday there was nothing. Minakshi replayed every chat in her head, wondering what she had said. Then the wondering turned hot. She typed three cutting messages in her notes app, read them back with a tight jaw, and sent none. After a night's sleep she wrote one line: "I miss talking to you. Did something happen?" Chandrika answered a week later with a short "busy, sorry," and in the corridor she laughed with her new dance group and gave Minakshi a nod, as if Minakshi were a poster on the wall. It stung. At the lockers Minakshi said quietly, "It feels like you've moved on and I'm background now," and Chandrika shrugged and said friendships change. Minakshi nodded and stopped checking her phone for Chandrika's name. She joined the library club and began sitting with two girls who saved her a seat. Meanwhile Vishal, the boy she was seeing, replied only when it suited him and left her waiting for hours. She told him, "I need an answer by evening, even a short one." When nothing changed after two weeks, she told him she was stepping back.

qa.q: What was Chandrika's last reply on Monday?
qa.a: Chandrika's last reply was a thumbs-up.

qa.q: How did Minakshi's approach to Chandrika's silence differ from her approach to Vishal's slow replies?
qa.a: With Chandrika she sent one honest message, named the feeling once and then stopped chasing; with Vishal she said what she needed, and when nothing changed after two weeks she stepped back.

qa.q: What was Minakshi feeling when she typed the three cutting messages?
qa.a: She felt furious and hurt, with a tight jaw, but she chose not to send them.

qa.q: What could Minakshi do next to build friendships that go both ways?
qa.a: She could keep sitting with the two girls at the library club, who saved her a seat, and put her energy into friends who answer back.

grounding: One teenager is ghosted by a friend and slowly dropped by a best friend, then meets slow replies from a partner, and handles each with a different calm step.

passage: Dilnaz caught herself rolling her eyes again as Kashish took a long time to finish her slide in Tuesday's meeting. Dilnaz was tense: she and Rehana were both up for the same senior post, and she kept a private tally of every win Rehana had. That night she saw that the eye-roll had more to do with her own stress and pride than with Kashish. Next day she offered to sit with her for twenty minutes over the spreadsheet and agreed a clear time for handing over. She also stayed late on her own launch report, so the results showed on the dashboard. On Thursday Dilnaz's father was taken to hospital in the middle of launch week. She rang the office from the corridor, shaking. Kashish took her deck to the client call and finished the tests without being asked. Rehana, to Dilnaz's surprise, forwarded her own notes. Dilnaz had noticed a typo in Rehana's section of the shared draft and had been tempted to leave it for the boss to find, but she told Rehana directly instead. A week later Dilnaz brought Kashish coffee, thanked her in front of the team, and covered her when Kashish went to an appointment.

qa.q: Where was Dilnaz's father taken on Thursday?
qa.a: He was taken to hospital.

qa.q: How did Dilnaz's view of Kashish change, and what did Kashish's help show about working together?
qa.a: Dilnaz first rolled her eyes because Kashish was slow, then saw the contempt came from her own stress and pride and offered help with clear timing; later Kashish covered for her in an emergency, showing that mutual help matters more than any single task.

qa.q: What was Dilnaz feeling when she rang the office from the corridor?
qa.a: She felt frightened and overwhelmed, since she was shaking with her father in hospital during launch week.

qa.q: How could Dilnaz keep the rivalry with Rehana healthy?
qa.a: She could keep focusing on her own visible results, stay honest and never sabotage Rehana, letting the rivalry sharpen her work.

grounding: A young professional's rivalry for a promotion, contempt for a slower colleague and gratitude for emergency cover show three different workplace stances.

passage: Parul's mother, Ganga, called three times a day to ask where she was, and had asked to see her bank messages "just to be safe." Her father paid the hostel fees, and both parents used money like a leash: "If you skip the coaching class, we will hold back your allowance." Parul felt she could not say what she thought. Once she booked the wrong date for her train home and paid the change fee herself; Ganga only said, "You'll remember next time." That month her parents' arguments started again, and each sent Parul long messages about the other. She felt caught between them and wanted to pick a side. Instead she told both, "I love you and I can't fix this. Please don't send me each other's words." She sat down with her mother and said, "Let's agree on a monthly budget, and I'll send a spending summary on Sundays. And I want to try a part-time job." Ganga hesitated, then said she was scared. Parul's roommate Leela told her about a weekend library job. Parul took it and began managing her own money, and she stopped buying takeaways she did not need. Ganga stopped asking for her messages once the Sunday summary arrived.

qa.q: What job did Leela tell Parul about?
qa.a: Leela told Parul about a weekend library job.

qa.q: How did Parul's handling of her parents' fights differ from how she handled her mother's control over money?
qa.a: With the fights she refused to take a side and said she loved both and could not fix it; with the money control she negotiated a monthly budget with Sunday summaries and began earning.

qa.q: What was Ganga feeling when she hesitated and said she was scared?
qa.a: She felt anxious and afraid for Parul, and her worry was behind the checking.

qa.q: What could Parul do next to keep support from turning into control?
qa.a: She could keep the budget and the summaries, keep earning, and speak honestly with her parents instead of lying or manipulating them for money.

grounding: One student sees protective worry, parental conflict, financial control and money dependence around the same family and answers each with honest boundaries.

passage: Himani, two years old, sat on the sofa with the phone propped in front of her, her face gone still and her mouth a little open as bright colours flashed. Her father, Yash, was chopping onions and had handed it over so she would stay quiet. She did not look up when he spoke to her, or when the pan hissed. When Yash gently lifted the phone away, she screamed and reached for it with both hands. Her uncle Eshaan, visiting, saw the screen go dark and Himani fling herself flat on the floor, heels drumming. He sat beside her and kept his voice low. "You're sad. The phone is finished now." He did not give it back. He opened his arms, and she sobbed into his shoulder for a minute. Then he rattled a tin of wooden spoons and small pots and said, "Shall we make soup?" Himani gave a hiccup and stirred with a spoon. Afterwards Yash sat cross-legged with her on the floor and named the pots as she banged them. That evening they watched one short video together, and Yash talked about the animals on the screen and asked her to point to the cow.

qa.q: What did Eshaan rattle to get Himani's attention?
qa.a: He rattled a tin of wooden spoons and small pots.

qa.q: How was the phone different when Yash handed it over to keep Himani quiet and when they watched the video at the end?
qa.a: When it was handed over to keep her quiet, Himani got bright colours but no person and screamed when it was taken; in the evening Yash watched one short video with her, talked about the animals and asked her to point to the cow, so the screen became a shared tool.

qa.q: What was Himani feeling when she flung herself on the floor?
qa.a: She felt sad and frustrated, not naughty, which showed in her drumming heels and her sobbing into Eshaan's shoulder.

qa.q: What could Yash do next time he needs to cook while Himani is nearby?
qa.a: He could give her a tin of spoons and small pots to play with beside him and keep the phone for shared moments.

grounding: A toddler's phone use is seen as absorbed handover, screaming when it is removed, and a calm limit with a hug and new play from a caregiver.

passage: The envelope from the tax office made Uma's heart race, and for an hour she imagined the worst. Then she sat down, read it slowly twice, wrote the reply date on a sticky note and started pulling out invoices. The whole thing felt unfair to her: the forms were tangled and she hated paying so much. "You can grumble at the system and still follow it," said Jaya. "Vote, write to your representative, but file." That evening Bhupen, a friend of a cousin, phoned. "Give me a fee and a little extra for a clerk, and this whole notice will disappear." Uma's stomach sank. She said no, thanked him and hung up. Jaya gave her the name of a certified accountant. Uma booked an appointment, brought her documents and asked for a receipt for every payment. She treated the notice as a set of rules to work through, not an attack, and wrote her reply in polite, accurate language, sending it two days before the date on the sticky note. Afterwards she still muttered about the system, but she slept properly that night.

qa.q: What did Uma write on a sticky note?
qa.a: She wrote the reply date on a sticky note.

qa.q: How did Uma's response to Bhupen's offer differ from how she handled the notice itself?
qa.a: Bhupen offered to make the notice disappear for a fee and a little extra, a shortcut she refused, while for the notice she read it slowly, gathered documents, saw a certified accountant, asked for receipts and replied politely before the date.

qa.q: What was Uma feeling when the envelope from the tax office arrived?
qa.a: She felt frightened, since her heart raced and she imagined the worst.

qa.q: What could Uma do if she keeps feeling the system is unfair?
qa.a: She could keep following the rules while voting or writing to her representative, as Jaya suggested. 🙂

grounding: One young adult's tax notice brings fear, an agent's shortcut offer, resentment of the system and a calm, respectful reply.

passage: After Bidisha's project won the company award, messages poured in. Siddharth, who had never spoken to her at work, called her a genius and within a minute asked her to look at his proposal before anyone else's. She thanked him, remembered he had ignored her question last year, and said she would get to it after her own deadline. Zubin, her old college friend, congratulated her over tea, then grinned, "Look at the big shot now." Bidisha kept quiet about her raise, asked about his new job, and said she still owed him for the notes he lent her in second year. He softened a little. That night she lay awake thinking she had been lucky and that someone would find out. She opened a folder where she kept feedback and finished tasks, and asked her mentor to tell her plainly where she was weak. At the next town hall she was invited to speak. She named Tanmay for the data pipeline and Lata for the tests, said the bonus would be split with them, and emailed the director exactly what each had done.

qa.q: Who did Bidisha name for the data pipeline?
qa.a: She named Tanmay for the data pipeline.

qa.q: How did Bidisha's response to Siddharth's praise differ from her response to Zubin's teasing?
qa.a: She thanked Siddharth but remembered he had ignored her before and put his favour after her own deadline, while with Zubin she stayed humble, kept quiet about her raise and rooted the friendship in shared history and his news.

qa.q: What was Bidisha feeling as she lay awake that night?
qa.a: She felt anxious and doubtful, afraid that she had only been lucky and that someone would find out.

qa.q: What could Bidisha do next to stay grounded after her success?
qa.a: She could keep her folder of feedback, keep asking her mentor for plain feedback and keep learning without pretending to know everything.

grounding: After an award, one professional meets a sudden flatterer, an envious old friend, her own impostor fear and the chance to credit her team by name.
